_meta: A short agent plan of tool calls, one of which never returns, used to show that a harness which dispatches each tool call and waits with no per-call timeout freezes the entire agent on the first hung call -- every later step never runs and the run neither finishes nor errors -- while wrapping each call in a per-call timeout turns the hang into an ordinary error the loop can record and step past. An agent loop's tools are I/O: a network request, a subprocess, a database query, another model. Any of them can hang -- a dropped connection with no socket timeout, a deadlocked lock, a dependency that is simply down and holding the connection open. The naive loop calls the tool and blocks on the return, so a call that never returns blocks the loop forever: the agent is not crashed and not looping, it is wedged on one call, and no iteration cap or step budget helps because those count completed steps and this step never completes. The fix is a per-call timeout (a watchdog around each dispatch): if a tool has not returned within the budget, abort the wait and hand the loop a timeout error for that call, exactly as if the tool had raised. The agent then proceeds -- retry, try an alternative, or report the failure -- and the whole run stays bounded by n_calls times the timeout instead of being hostage to the slowest tool. Each call has a duration in milliseconds; a duration of null means the call never returns (it hangs). timeout_ms is the per-call budget. Calls that finish within the budget run to completion normally and are NOT aborted; only the over-budget call is turned into a timeout error. the plan, each call's duration, and the timeout are the fixture; whether the run completes, its total elapsed time, and each call's outcome under each strategy are computed. Stdlib only.
